orders.objective:

and sees the six works as a shelf, each with its title, its row count and the
scene it feeds. They choose AI for Games and see its chapters as a table of
contents with a concept count per chapter; they open Chapter 3 Movement and
see its sections and their concepts; they choose Two-level formation
steering and read, in a measure set for reading, its definition in full, its
type, its place in the book (part, chapter, section, subsection), its related
concepts as links in running text (Anchor point, Slot, Fixed formations), the
hook the map's author suggested for DotLn as a sentence, and, because the
tool is typed, its five faces rendered as one sentence (give it to a
formation of three or more units on terrain; it steers an anchor as a
character and the members to slots; watch the anchor-to-mean distance and
the slot error; measure the assignment cost) with its parameters and their
defaults. They follow Slot to its own reading and return. They type "arrive"
into the search and reach Arrive in two keystrokes and one click. On Arrive
they read that the soldier scene runs it, and once the scene exists a link
opens the scene with that tool chosen. Their last ten readings persist
across a reload. A concept whose definition the run marked as the mapping
worker's own reading says so beside the definition. Nothing on the page is a
label-value list with nothing to read. What the operator learns is what each
concept is and how a work hangs together; what they decide is which tool to
try in the scene.

orders.title: WO-015 — The soldier scene: twenty units on a 2D canvas behind a renderer seam, a rail of the tools the engine runs with each tool's definition read from the catalog, real-time-strategy selection, flock, arrive and a two-level formation with slot roles, a deterministic seeded clock, before-and-after trials, the first real look, the root route, and the pure scene engine every later scene reuses
orders.objective:
(the operator's session, WS-001 rule 24) the operator opens the app and lands
on `/scene`: twenty units idling on a dark field that fills the page below
the shell's header, each labelled with a lifecycle role and coloured by it;
a narrow rail on the right lists the tools the engine runs, grouped by what
they do (move: seek, arrive, wander; group: separation, cohesion, velocity
matching, flock; avoid: priority steering; form: wedge, line, column, with
two-level and fixed formation and slot roles), each name in its work's
colour; an instrument strip along the bottom shows cohesion radius,
collisions, heading variance, time to objective and stalled units at their
idle values beside the seed and the transport. They drag a marquee round
twelve units (or click, shift-click, double-click a squad, Escape to clear,
or Tab and Space through the text layer below the field). They choose Flock
in the rail and the inspector shows the catalog's definition of flocking in
a readable measure, its five faces as a sentence, its three weights as
sliders with defaults, and ghost arrows on the selected units showing the
first frame's accelerations. They apply: the twelve pull together and move
as a group, the cohesion radius falls, collisions stay at zero, and a
sparkline under each figure shows the change. They click the field to set an
objective and apply Arrive: the group slows and stops inside the target
radius. They select eight more and apply Formation: wedge; the units sort
themselves into slots, the hardest to place first, while the slot table in
the inspector fills from the cost table. They open Compare and see the
branch before the equip as a ghost under the branch after, two series per
metric, with the first divergence frame marked; they keep the trial. They
save the composition, reload, and find it. Under reduced motion the field is
still until they press Step or Play; the same seed and the same steps
reproduce the same frames; nothing leaves the browser. A tool opened from
the catalog's "runs in the soldier scene" link arrives chosen in the rail.
What the operator learns is what each movement idea does to a group when
they can see it; what they decide is which ideas to keep and which to try
on the agents next.

goalReview.goalStandard:
## Goal-aligned decisions

The [sequence](../planning/sequence.md) and selected work order determine
current placement and authority. The mission is the outcome; the critical path
is the dependency route to the next outcome. Useful prerequisite or
risk-reduction work must name the blocked outcome it enables. Process activity,
receipt volume and agent utilization are not progress by themselves. Goal
alignment grants no authority to reorder or expand work. In all phases, the Goal
Alignment and Process Cost procedure lives in the generated role skills
[WO-043, 2026-09-11].

Accuracy takes priority over agreement in every phase. The already-equipped
Correctness over Sycophancy rule applies to operator suggestions and the agent's
own premises equally: challenge unsupported claims, distinguish observation
from inference, state material uncertainty, and correct mistakes when evidence
changes. A confident request or an earlier decision is not proof of correctness.
Record material disagreement and its evidence in the same decision or phase
receipt; do not manufacture dissent or seek approval for ordinary judgment.

| Lens                                  | Decision question                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy resistance / fixes that fail   | Will local goals or guards undo one another?                                                              |
| Tragedy of the commons                | Does the solution consume shared compute, context or operator attention without accounting for the total? |
| Drift to low performance              | Does it improve an explicit outcome standard rather than normalize a worse baseline?                      |
| Escalation                            | Will additional process provoke more process or workarounds?                                              |
| Success to the successful             | Are credible alternatives excluded merely because the current mechanism already has investment?           |
| Shifting the burden to the intervenor | Does the solution remove recurring operator rescue or depend on it?                                       |
| Rule beating                          | Can the evidence pass without the intended behavior occurring?                                            |
| Seeking the wrong goal                | Does it advance operator flow and the selected product outcome rather than a proxy?                       |

Naive Interventionism adds the existing system's useful functions, affected
consumers, second-order harm, reversibility and smallest useful probe. NoOp
records what happens if nothing changes, why action or inaction wins, and the
evidence that would reopen the choice. Scale detail to consequence: explain
applicable risks and briefly group immaterial lenses with a reason; do not
manufacture eight repetitive paragraphs for routine edits.

Record evidence of benefit and the risks of intervening in existing behavior;
verification and handoff compare observed outcomes with the promised benefit.
Required legal or release actions retain their existing authority; NoOp is a
considered alternative, not an ambient veto or permission to abandon authorized
work.



Material choices and rationales go in existing phase evidence: per-order
`docs/evidence/WO-NNN/decisions.md` and cited product sections for work-order
decisions; planning dispositions/candidate records for planning choices; the
independent report or refutation receipt for its judgment; retained closeout
evidence for release decisions. The decisions index exposes per-order records.
Reuse and link a current rationale until its assumptions change; do not create
a parallel decision log or an extra approval ritual.


This launchpad is the operator's own DotLn instance. Its purpose is to plan and
run bounded, evidence-gated work orders across the operator's repositories, so
that every change arrives as a pull request the operator reads before it merges,
while the kit itself stays upstream and reaches this fork only through starter
updates. The first workstream is DotLn-Angular, an Nx and Angular monorepo that
serves two outcomes at once: the operator's reference Angular workspace, which a
colleague should recognize as the way the operator builds Angular, and the
operator's sandbox app, one app with sub-apps behind a menu: a scene for
authoring game AI from a toolbox mined from the works the operator reads, a
view of DotLn's machinery where a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what
changes in an example use case, the operator's own digital twin, and side
utilities. Every new idea lives there first as a toy the operator plays with
before promoting the ones that work, for the five UIFA roles, people and
software actors alike. The app is not wired to DotLn core: its data comes from
public mining into its own store, served to the UI through its own API, and it
informs the platform through GitHub issues, never by writing a control record,
so that the app improves the platform, the platform the starter, the starter
this fork, and the fork the app in turn. The critical path runs from registering
that repository in this launchpad, through one witnessed target order that
scaffolds the workspace, to a foundation where a feature is added by convention:
shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell,
and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model. Later
workstreams join the same way: one registration and one planning pass each,
with the fork's own machinery changes cut as self orders beside them.

episode.statement: Independent plan refuter (identity Entropy Reducer, mask Contra-Auguste, lens architecture-and-semantics) for the 2026-10-28 planning pass. I read only the canonical prompt file, in full: its identity, mask, lens, role, the refuter work order, the compiled subject (the standard; the goal review with its platform and goal standards, critical-path field and five trap observations; the five judged orders' titles, objectives, Cost lines, criteria and non-goals; the six-order sequence; the empty deferrals; and the cost table with its null per-order metrics and first-verification fold), the output instructions, the result schema and the worker instructions. I read no repository files, planning documents, receipts or Git history and ran no model tools. The prompt named the mask without defining it. The subject marked the vision, the UIFA roles document and the capability table unavailable, so no vision passage ids were supplied and the five roles could not be judged against a roles table. For WO-015, WO-016, WO-008, WO-017 and WO-018 I answered all four questions. (1) Critical-path gate and recorded NoOp cost: no NoOp cost is recorded for any order, because the metrics are null and there are no acceptances. (2) All eight system traps against each order's own process cost. (3) Whether the Cost line names a removal larger than the addition: none does; two arriving pages are removed against about 292 source files added. (4) Whether failure degrades to the old behaviour: mostly yes in the browser, with refusals noted for WO-015's root redirect, WO-017's base-commit check and permission-gated twin route, and WO-018's fan-out stop rule. Verdicts: WO-015 aligned-with-findings, WO-016 aligned-with-findings, WO-008 aligned-with-findings, WO-017 aligned-with-findings, WO-018 aligned-with-findings; plan verdict aligned-with-findings. Holds: 0, because every trap observation reports no worsening, no judged order has run, and no vision passage id was supplied. Known issues: 13, each with a concrete reopening observation. They include: the subject disagreeing with itself about whether a critical path is declared; the refutation cost already paid on these texts (28 refutations across the five orders, twelve of them on WO-008); a tension between WO-016's source commit and its hex scrub; the twin route being unreachable in a production build that has no identity provider; and worker read observations admitted as unobserved in WO-018. Findings confer no operator decision authority. I made no repository or Git writes and committed no receipt.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No declared critical path; against the mission's route WO-019 closes no foundation gate. It reworks WO-014's sandbox content into what the next product order needs: WO-015's Objective and criterion 1 require the inspector to show the catalog's definition of flocking, and WO-014's allow-list forbids definitions in the data, so WO-019 is a prerequisite that names its blocked outcome (the soldier scene reading a catalog that serves it, the steering, formation and objective tools typed). It also gives WO-018 the join and the v1 schema it extends. NoOp cost in the records: none recorded (the WO-019 row's metrics are null). Inferred NoOp: WO-014's allow-list stays, WO-015 criterion 1 cannot be met without reopening this order or loosening WO-015, and the catalog stays the label-value surface this order's Objective rejects. Action wins on the dependency; the evidence that would reopen the choice is WO-015's walkthrough reading definitions that did not come from this join.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the order is the reversal of WO-014's guard (allow-list, scrub call over catalog strings, with-definition fixture) and adds a missing-definition fixture pointing the other way; if the scrub also carried non-copyright protections (absolute paths, private terms), those go with it (finding). Tragedy of the commons: the join is a script, not a model fan-out, so regenerating 3,463 rows should cost a fraction of WO-014's 117.7M tokens (row:WO-014); unknown until run. Full definitions, relations and hooks on every row grow the lazy catalog data that every later bundle budget shares. Drift to low performance: criterion 7 holds the declared budgets; the risk is a budget raised to admit larger data rather than the data split (finding). Escalation: the LayoutSide or LayoutStrip pick adds an operator decision at the pull request and a removal step before final review. Success to the successful: the mission places the app's data in its own store served through its own API, yet the mining store and HTTP API (C1) stay deferred while the bundled JSON takes a second schema version. Shifting the burden: the pick is a designed decision, not a rescue; acceptance by walkthrough moves work to the verifier. Rule beating: walkthrough evidence is a file count (at least 9) and the layout test is a line count of the substring 'Layout' (prints 1); both can pass or fail apart from the behaviour (findings). Seeking the wrong goal: criterion 1 tests the operator's reading session itself, the outcome rather than a proxy, and requires the verifier to state from the page alone what two concepts are.
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes the tool-list and tool-faces composites, the with-definition.json negative fixture and the scrub call over catalog strings; it adds join-maps.mjs, catalog:join, the tool-v1 schema, a rebuilt catalog page (layout, shelf, contents, reading pane, faces sentence, search, history, mappers, facade, stories), events and persisted state, a missing-definition fixture, rewritten e2e, baselines, documents and translations: about 35 source files plus regenerated data that now carries full text per row. The removal is a guard and two composites; the addition is a reading surface and a larger dataset. It is the only order in the horizon whose removal is more than a placeholder page, and it reduces entropy only if the guard's non-copyright functions survive.
orders.failureBehavior: Partly. A relation whose target is absent has a null id and renders as text (criterion 4 checks only non-null ids), and a definition the run marked as the worker's own reading is labelled rather than hidden; both degrade. The check refuses any row without a definition and a place.chapter (criterion 2), so a map row the run left without a definition fails the join instead of falling back to WO-014's typed-only row: a refusal where the old behaviour admitted. The persisted history (last ten readings) has no stated spec for an unparseable value or an id the regenerated data no longer carries, although WO-015, WO-016 and WO-017 each state one. With the scrub call gone, a string it would have refused is admitted with no fallback.

findings.reason: Flagged as suspect material for operator judgment. Criterion 8 requires docs/ai-reference/catalog-rules.md to state that the clean room does not govern the works the operator references, and the order commits the run's definitions, relations and hooks for six works that WO-014 kept out as intake and whose copying WO-014's non-goals forbade. A rules file read by the target's agents that scopes the clean room speaks to a floor my work order records as locked. Whether model-written definitions of these works' concepts are the owner's to publish is a provenance judgment for the operator, not a finding of fact here; WO-018, by contrast, records its public text's source and SHA-256. Not a hold: no vision passage id was supplied and no observation records a failure.

findings.reason: Naive intervention on a guard with more than one function. Criterion 2 removes the scrub call over catalog strings (grep for assertScrubbed prints nothing) and WO-019's check keeps no stated rule for absolute paths, which WO-014's summary rule carried ('no absolute path'). The hooks are the map author's suggestions for DotLn and are the strings most likely to name local paths or private terms. If the scrub carried those checks, failure no longer degrades to the old behaviour; it removes it.

findings.reason: The scene-tool contract is underspecified across the WO-019 to WO-015 seam. Criterion 3 types the aifg scene tools with five kinds (steer.blend, steer.priority, formation.twoLevel, formation.fixed, objective.set); WO-015's rail names seek, arrive, wander, separation, cohesion, velocity matching, flock, priority steering, wedge, line, column, two-level and fixed formation and slot roles; this order's own Objective has Arrive say that the soldier scene runs it. The visible text does not say which of the five kinds Arrive, Seek or Wander carry, and 'step 5' and 'step 8's floor' are not in the compiled subject.

A story title, import or comment containing 'Layout' fails a correct result; renaming the losing story or leaving its component outside the stories file passes an incorrect one. WO-015 criterion 7 states the same requirement for the chrome pick with no command at all, so the two sibling orders test one convention two ways.

findings.reason: The acceptance-by-use criteria (this order and WO-015, WO-016, WO-008, WO-017, WO-018) prove the screenshots by file count (ls | wc -l at least 9 or 12). The dated steps and the verifier's own-words statement carry the real test; the count can be met by any files. The six walkthroughs also add at least 69 screenshot files under docs/evidence, a per-order growth no Cost line names.

The last ten readings persist across a reload, but no criterion states what an unparseable stored value or a stored id absent from the regenerated data does; WO-015, WO-016 and WO-017 each carry such a spec. Regeneration by catalog:join is exactly the event that can orphan stored ids.

Every row now carries a full definition, relations, hooks and a place; criterion 7 keeps the declared budgets but nothing records the catalog chunk size against WO-014's recorded figure, and WO-018 adds another work with no budget criterion of its own. The easy repair under pressure is a raised budget, which normalizes a worse baseline.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: the subject's criticalPath field says this instance has not declared a critical path, while the goal standard's prose names one (registration, one witnessed scaffold, then a foundation of shared libraries, the component taxonomy, events and stores, the sub-app shell and a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model). Against that prose WO-015 contributes one shared library (libs/shared/scene-engine, the pure engine later scenes reuse) and one taxonomy sentence (a wrapper may own a browser drawing API, c9). Beyond that it is the first sandbox outcome the vision names, the scene for authoring game AI, and the new root landing. It depends on WO-019's typed scene tools and catalog definitions and sits second in the sequence. NoOp in the records: the cost table's WO-015 row has metrics null and the acceptances list is empty, so the records hold no NoOp cost. The NoOp state the Cost line implies is that /scene stays WO-013's arriving page and the root keeps redirecting to /board, so the operator still cannot watch a movement idea act on a group. The cost is unknown, and unknown is not a structural hold.
orders.systemTraps: Rule beating: the evidence is mostly behavioural. It rests on the operator's session performed by the verifier with their own statement of cohesion radius, collisions and time to objective (c1); seeded determinism, the separation-at-zero collision spec and the first-divergence spec (c2); and every rail entry's kind asserted against the interpreter's set (c5). Weak points: the greedy slot table is 'hand-computed' but committed by the executor whose code it checks; the '<dl|dotln-key-value-list' grep (c7) is a markup proxy that a label-value layout built from other elements passes, and only the walkthrough screenshots back it (finding). Shifting the burden / tragedy of the commons: c7 makes the operator pick in every design comparison round, with no cap on rounds. Operator attention is the shared resource this order spends most. The shifting-the-burden series records operator directions of 1, 4, 1, 3 and 6, with WO-014, the latest order, at the maximum (finding). Seeking the wrong goal: aligned. Acceptance is the operator's own session, not a proxy, and the non-goals refuse a DotLn analog claim from a flock. Drift to low performance: about 180 KB of context against an executor cold start that rose from 29,364 to 29,978 bytes with no ceiling set; 17 steps; gate step count flat at 7. Escalation: three refutations paid; ten criteria; no command added in the target, so process grows only by criteria. Policy resistance: guard-refusal series 0 or null. The 'exactly one chrome story, no rejected branch' rule could push the executor to delete design evidence, but the screenshots under design/ and the decisions file keep the comparison. Success to the successful: the 2D canvas without a rendering dependency is fixed by non-goal, while the renderer seam (Canvas, Text and Null implementations, c3) keeps alternatives open, so there is no lock-in.
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes WO-013's arriving page for /scene and moves the root redirect from /board to /scene. It adds libs/shared/scene-engine, the scene feature (page, layout, rail, inspector, text layer, canvas wrapper, log, trial compare, facade, store, clock, tokens), the field skin's token layer, four fixtures, a fixture check, two documents, one taxonomy sentence and about 70 source files. The addition is far larger than the removal. For a first sandbox sub-app that is expected, but the identity's question is answered no.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades. An uninterpreted step is refused with a reason, while the next frame's hash and the clock's tick count equal those of a run without that step (c2). A stored value that does not parse, or has an older shape, yields the idle twenty units (c6). An unknown or refused tool id arrives with no tool chosen and a visible notice naming why (c5). Reduced motion keeps the field still until Step or Play. One path does not degrade: the root redirect moves from /board to /scene and the wildcard page's home link follows it, so a scene that fails to load leaves the root without the old /board landing. The criteria verify only the success path (finding).

findings.reason: c7 requires the decisions file to record every comparison round's pair and the operator's pick, with no limit on rounds. Each round spends operator attention, the resource the shifting-the-burden series tracks; WO-014 drew 6 operator directions, the highest in the series. The order's Cost line counts executor hours, context bytes and steps but not operator rounds, so the total operator cost is unaccounted.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-015's decisions file records more than six comparison rounds, or the cost table records WO-015's operator directions above WO-014's 6.

findings.reason: The grep for '<dl|dotln-key-value-list' stands in for the rule 'no label-value list on the scene'. A label-value layout built from other elements passes it, so the evidence can pass without the intended behaviour; only the walkthrough screenshots check the rendered page. WO-008 c8 and WO-018 c6 use the same proxy.
findings.reopenWhen: A walkthrough screenshot under docs/evidence/WO-015/walkthrough/ (or WO-008's or WO-018's) shows a label-value list on a page whose grep printed nothing.

findings.reason: Moving the root redirect and the wildcard home link to /scene makes the scene's lazy chunk and engine the app's entry point. The criteria assert only that the root lands on /scene, not what the root shows if the scene fails, so this path refuses rather than degrading to the old /board landing.
findings.reopenWhen: An e2e run, a walkthrough or the operator records the root failing to render /scene while /board still serves.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: the shared-libraries member of the foundation the goal standard's prose names: libs/shared/records (reader, folds, fixture pack, kit) and libs/shared/replay (the virtual-time clock). WO-017 consumes both (its context reads 'the records and replay libraries'), so WO-016 sits on WO-017's dependency route, not on WO-008's. It also delivers the sandbox outcome the vision names: 'a view of DotLn's machinery where a change to an agent's mechanisms shows what changes in an example use case'. NoOp in the records: metrics null and no acceptances, so the records hold no NoOp cost. The implied NoOp is /machinery staying WO-013's arriving page and WO-017 lacking the libraries it reads. The cost is unknown, and unknown is not a structural hold.
orders.systemTraps: Rule beating: c2 pins exact fold figures: eight operator beats, and gaps of 87.8, 109.9, 1.7, 1.4, 2.1, 18.2 and 5.9 minutes, which sum to 227.0 and agree with WO-017's waiting total. c10 requires the verifier's own statement of what the applied idea changed. c3's role-count spec compares against counts the same executor recorded, so by itself it can pass without the intended behaviour, but the verifier's independent recount of each Origin stamp closes that gap. Seeking the wrong goal: the presentation-only band, the 'nothing written' caption, and the rule that no card is generated from records (c4, c8) keep the view from posing as a control surface, which matches the vision's 'never by writing a control record'. Shifting the burden: ideas persist in browser storage and, when the operator runs the sink, in an ignored intake directory. Moving them on to planning or a GitHub issue stays a manual operator step; the vision promises no automatic path, so none is owed. Tragedy of the commons: adds a long-running local process (npm run idea-sink) and about 190 KB of context; five refutations paid. Drift to low performance: 17 steps and ten criteria. Cold-start bytes rose for every role profile in the drift series with no ceiling; this order neither causes nor improves that. Escalation: one new target command and one new local service with its own refusal rules (Origin, Host, 16 KB body limit, ignored directory, Git root), all bounded by the c5 tooling test. Policy resistance: the scrub rule and the source.commit requirement in c1 can work against each other (finding). Success to the successful: WO-221 and WO-226 are reused because they are recorded; carrying a second order guards against fitting the fold to one segment. Clean room: the fixtures copy the platform's recorded segments, reduced to six fields and scrubbed. The scrub's stated patterns do not cover every private identifier shape (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes WO-013's arriving page for /machinery. It adds machinery.ts to the shared models, two shared libraries (records, replay), the machinery feature (page, strip, slots, cards, shelf, editor, facade, store), a data-access library, the segment reducer, a record fixture check, the idea sink process and its command, three fixtures, two documents and about 75 source files. The addition is far larger than the removal.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades. A failing sink post still applies and persists the dropped idea (c6). A stored value that does not parse renders an empty shelf and the strip (c6). An unknown row type becomes an unknown beat, and a planner, refuter or release-close row becomes an unknown-slot beat naming the role (c2). A refused drop stays visible with its reason and leaves the scene unchanged (c2, c7). The sink refuses to start on a directory that is not Git-ignored or lies outside its Git root. That is a refusal, but it is the safety boundary of a local write, and the browser path continues without the sink; production sets ideaSinkUrl to null and ships no loopback address (c5).

findings.reason: c1 requires each segment fixture to carry a source.commit, and it requires the reducer's scrub to fail any value carrying a run of 32 or more hexadecimal characters. A full Git commit id is 40 hexadecimal characters. Either source.commit is exempt from the scrub or the commit must be abbreviated, and the criterion says neither, so the executor and the verifier can read the same text differently.
findings.reopenWhen: The executor's fixture carries a 40-character source.commit and npm run check:fixtures or the scrub's tooling test rejects it, or the decisions file records an exemption or abbreviation for source.commit.

findings.reason: The scrub's stated patterns are hex runs of 32 or more characters, UUID shapes and absolute paths. They do not cover e-mail addresses, host names or account names. The kept fields include actor, which the objective labels by harness, model and effort, and the subject does not show what actor carries in the platform's segments. The vision says the app's data comes from public mining into its own store; the subject does not establish that these copied segments are publishable.
findings.reopenWhen: Any value in order-221.json or order-226.json is observed carrying an e-mail address, a host name or an account identifier, or the source segments are observed to come from records the owner cannot publish.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: the last member of the foundation the goal standard's prose names, 'a legitimate client-side authentication and permission model', so it is the only judged order that closes a named critical-path gate. It also unblocks WO-017, whose /twin maps to twin:read and whose e2e signs in through this order's mocked provider. The subject's criticalPath field reports no declared critical path, and the sequence places WO-008 fourth, behind WO-019, WO-015 and WO-016 (finding). c4 requires the board, scene, machinery and catalog e2e specs to run unchanged without a session, which bounds the cost of that ordering. NoOp in the records: metrics null and no acceptances, so the records hold no NoOp cost. The implied NoOp is no session, no permission model and no consumer for WO-017's twin:read. The cost is unknown, and unknown is not a structural hold.
orders.systemTraps: Rule beating: strong. The post-sign-in e2e reads every Web Storage key, IndexedDB object store, Cache Storage entry and cookie, checking for the JWT shape and for every token the mock issued (c1). The transition spec iterates the full state and event table (c2). Single-flight refresh is asserted through the MSW handler's call count (c3). The production bundle is grepped for the kid and the mock marker (c5). The reload criterion accepts either keeping the session or returning to /login with returnTo, so it proves only that a reload never strands the visitor; with tokens held only in memory, that is the honest bound. c8's '<dl' grep is the same markup proxy noted on WO-015. Seeking the wrong goal: the order is security shape rather than operator flow, but it is the named foundation member, and c6 records that the server enforces authorization while client checks shape presentation only, which is what 'legitimate' requires. Shifting the burden: c8's walkthrough drives knobs in the mocked build, and no recurring operator step follows the order. Tragedy of the commons and escalation: the decisive process cost is planning, not execution. Eleven refutation receipts (001 to 011) name this order and this pass is the twelfth, against a platform standard that says the refutation pass must be made worth its cost before a later pass pays it again. The shifting-the-burden observation lists twelve planning captures from 2026-10-18 to 2026-10-28 (finding). Drift to low performance: about 160 KB of context, 15 steps, eight criteria. Policy resistance: in-memory tokens, cross-tab sign-out and the ban on localStorage and sessionStorage in house code are compatible (a broadcast channel suffices); guard-refusal series 0 or null. Success to the successful: one OIDC client library behind a port; the port keeps the library replaceable, and the provider swap is configuration only.
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing. It adds libs/shared/auth with its kit, the mocked identity provider handlers, two event groups, guards, a permission directive, three routes (/login, /denied, /account) and about 60 source files. It also adds one runtime dependency, an OpenID Connect client library and the only runtime dependency the horizon adds, plus jose as a development dependency.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades where it should and refuses where credentials require it. With auth at null, the four public routes admit an anonymous visitor and /login renders the unavailable state (c5), and the board, scene, machinery and catalog specs run unchanged without a session (c4), which is the old behaviour. Refresh failure and an invalid signature, audience or skew sign the visitor out to /login, the correct fail-closed path for tokens. One consequence for later orders: production carries no mock and a real provider is a non-goal, so in the production build any permission-gated route refuses (see WO-017).

findings.reason: This is a plan-level process cost, attached to WO-008 because it carries the most. WO-008's Cost line records eleven refutation receipts plus this pass's judgment on an order that has not run. Across the five judged orders, the Cost lines record 28 refutations paid (3, 5, 12, 5 and 3). The shifting-the-burden observation lists twelve planning captures in eleven days, and its operator-direction series reached 6 at WO-014. The goal standard says process activity is not progress, and the platform standard says the point is a platform, not proof of every constructible case before filing. This pass finds no observed failure, so repeating judgment on unchanged texts would spend cost without new evidence.
findings.reopenWhen: A later planning pass commits a refutation receipt naming WO-008 while WO-008's text and the cost table's trap observations are unchanged from this pass's evidence, or WO-008's run records a failure that one of its earlier refutations would have caught.

findings.reason: Two parts of the subject disagree. The criticalPath field says this instance has not declared a critical path, while the goal standard's prose declares one that ends at the client-side authentication and permission model. Under the prose, WO-008 is the only judged order that closes a named gate, yet it is sequenced after three feature orders; under the field, no judged order can be said to unblock any gate. The plan's first question therefore has no single source of truth. Goal alignment grants no authority to reorder, so this is reported, not acted on, and c4's unchanged-e2e rule bounds the ordering's cost.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-015 or WO-016 records a decision, rework or route change caused by the missing permission model, or WO-008's run changes an earlier feature's route or e2e spec beyond its routePermissions entry.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: no member of the stated foundation. It is the first feature to consume the permission model (twin:read on BasePaths.Twin and the default user's claim), so it shows the foundation's 'feature added by convention' for permissions, and it delivers the vision's 'operator's own digital twin'. It depends on WO-016 (the records and replay libraries) and on WO-008 (the mocked provider and routePermissions), and the sequence respects both. NoOp in the records: metrics null and no acceptances, so the records hold no NoOp cost. The implied NoOp is no twin, with /account remaining the permission model's only gated consumer. The cost is unknown, and unknown is not a structural hold.
orders.systemTraps: Seeking the wrong goal: explicitly guarded. The twin is judged by the replayed order's results (virtual close, waiting minutes and early fires, set against 1,110.3 and 227.0 minutes) and never by agreement with the operator's beats; c3 enforces that with a vm field-set spec and a 'hit rate|tolerance band' grep. Rule beating: the baseline replay must reproduce the recorded close within one virtual second, and the derivation script must equal the fold (c1, c2), so the figures cannot pass without the replay working. c3's grep is a proxy, but the field-set spec carries the weight. Policy resistance: the permission gate on /twin serves a local goal, exercising WO-008, and works against the operator using the twin in the production build, which has no provider (finding). Drift to low performance and escalation: 'every variant kept, never deleted', plus a check that fails on a removed id, makes the registry grow by policy. Each variant is a lazy chunk and c8 checks budgets, but no removal path exists (finding). Shifting the burden: a graduated idea goes to core as a GitHub issue filed by hand, consistent with the vision. Tragedy of the commons: about 170 KB of context, 6 to 9 hours, five refutations paid, two new commands. Success to the successful: RxJS on virtual time is chosen because the RxJS that describes the operator is the RxJS that runs. Exporting generated TypeScript instead of interpreting JSON (c5) is a deliberate, coherent architecture, not inertia.
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing. It adds libs/shared/twin-model (variants, registry, results fold), the twin feature (page, lanes, picker, flips, result cell, facade, store), a derivation script and fixture, the variant registry check, a routePermissions entry, a provider claim, two documents, about 55 source files and two commands (twin:derive, twin:check). Its never-delete rule also forbids future removal inside the registry.
orders.failureBehavior: In the browser it degrades: a stored value that does not parse, or one naming an unknown variant, yields the first registry entry with no flips (c6). Two mechanisms refuse instead. First, twin:check fails when the base commit is absent (c4), deliberately and with a message naming the fetch; because c9 needs a passing row for every declared command, a shallow or pruned checkout fails the gate rather than degrading. Second, /twin requires twin:read, so without a session, and in a production build that carries neither the mock nor a real provider, the route lands on /login or /denied rather than on the old behaviour.

findings.reason: WO-008 keeps the mock out of the production build and makes a real provider a non-goal, so the production configuration has no identity provider. WO-017 maps /twin to twin:read, and for that reason its use walkthrough runs on the mocked configuration. The operator's served production app therefore cannot open the twin, unlike /scene, /machinery and Tools, whose walkthroughs run in production. The vision describes the twin as a sub-app the operator plays with.
findings.reopenWhen: The served production build is observed sending the operator to /login (unavailable) or /denied at /twin, or the operator records that the twin must open in the production build.

findings.reason: twin:check fails, not passes, when the base commit is absent. c9 requires a passing row for every declared command in the target gate, so a shallow clone or a pruned base turns a never-delete safeguard into a gate refusal rather than a degraded pass with a warning.
findings.reopenWhen: A target gate, verifier or CI run records twin:check failing for an absent base commit.

findings.reason: Every variant is kept as code, old versions are never deleted, and the registry check fails a manifest with a removed id. The registry, the lazy chunks and the picker can therefore only grow. This adds entropy by policy with no recorded ceiling on variant count or total twin bytes; c8 checks only each chunk against its own budget.
findings.reopenWhen: The production build's budget output names a twin chunk over budget, or the operator directs a variant's removal and twin:check refuses it.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: Gate: no member of the stated foundation. It delivers the vision's 'data comes from public mining into its own store' for one work and the toy shelf where 'every new idea lives there first as a toy', and it types the tactics a later commander scene needs. It depends on WO-019's catalog pipeline and rules ('the catalog rules as WO-019 leaves them'). NoOp in the records: metrics null and no acceptances, so the records hold no NoOp cost. The implied NoOp is a catalog without The Art of War, with the operator reading the run's toys outside the app to choose the next build. The cost is unknown, and unknown is not a structural hold.
orders.systemTraps: Tragedy of the commons: the only order with a fan-out (two fan-outs, at most twelve workers), and it accounts for it. c5 records per-worker token totals, the session's own total, a stop decision if the sum passes WO-014's recorded total, and the harness's subagent count; twelve stays under the default subagent cap of 20. Rule beating: c5 accepts each worker's own statement that no quarantine file was read and admits 'unobserved' as the launchpad's read observation, so the clean-room evidence can pass with no observation behind it (finding). Seeking the wrong goal: aligned. The walkthrough ends with the operator deciding the next toy, and the graduation route stays a GitHub issue. Shifting the burden: the operator files the 'build next' issue by hand, and issue export is a non-goal (candidate C4). Drift to low performance: about 190 KB of executor context, 14 steps and about 300 data rows. Escalation: one new command; catalog:check and catalog:join are reused. Policy resistance: the fan-out stop rule and the completeness criteria (thirteen chapters, 25 toys) can work against each other (finding). Success to the successful: tools are typed through the existing catalog pipeline rather than a new one, which is reuse, not lock-in. Clean room: the six new toys type tools from works that are not in the public domain (Meadows, Pirsig, Gladwell, Taleb), and the nineteen toys are carried 'in full' from the run's folder. The criteria check structure, the public text's source and SHA-256, and that a maxim appears only for the public text; they do not check that definitions drawn from non-public works are written in the owner's own words (finding).
orders.removalBalance: No. It removes nothing. It adds two catalog data files, a toy schema and model, toys.json with 25 records, toy-source tool files, the toy shelf and toy page, map and toy checks, two document sections, about 32 source files, about 300 data rows and one command (toys:check).
orders.failureBehavior: At check time it refuses, appropriately: a toy naming an unknown tool id fails toys:check, and the map check fails rows that lack required fields. At run time the subject states no fallback for the shelf or the toy page. In the process, the fan-out stop rule has no degraded acceptance: stopping on budget leaves the thirteen chapters or the 25 toys short, which fails c2 or c4 instead of shipping a partial mining. The stop threshold is WO-014's recorded order total, which this subject's cost table does not show (finding).

findings.reason: The clean-room evidence for the fan-out rests on each worker's own statement that no quarantine file was read. The launchpad's read observation beside it may be 'unobserved', so the criterion can pass without any observation that the intended behaviour occurred.
findings.reopenWhen: WO-018's evidence README records any worker's read observation as 'unobserved', or a non-zero harness journal row count for the quarantine path.

findings.reason: The stop rule (stop the fan-out if the token sum passes WO-014's recorded order total) has no degraded acceptance path, because c2 requires all thirteen chapters and c4 all 25 toys; a stop refuses the order instead of shipping part of the mining. The threshold depends on a recorded WO-014 token total, and this subject's cost table carries no token figures for any order.
findings.reopenWhen: The fan-outs' token sum passes WO-014's recorded order total before thirteen chapters are mapped, or WO-014's order token total is unavailable when the fan-out starts.

findings.reason: The six new toys' tools are 'typed from the work' for sources that are not in the public domain, and the nineteen toys enter 'in full' from the run's folder. c4 checks only that each public-work tool carries a definition and a source string, and c7 limits verbatim maxims to the public text. No criterion confirms that definitions drawn from non-public works are the owner's own words, or that the Art of War translation used is in the public domain.
findings.reopenWhen: Any toys.json record or tool definition is observed carrying verbatim text from a work not in the public domain, or the recorded Art of War source is a translation still under copyright.
